name: Glycine
summary: Glycine is a normal amino acid found in proteins and made by the body. It also takes part in making other molecules; selling it as a supplement does not mean that everyone has too little.
commonUses: Used in products marketed for sleep
Used in amino-acid and glutathione-support products
roles: Glycine is a building block for proteins and for glutathione.
It participates in one-carbon metabolism, the transfer of small chemical units used to make and maintain other molecules.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test. Lower blood glycine in some research populations does not establish a general dietary deficiency syndrome or a need for supplements.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

foodSources.note: Glycine occurs in dietary proteins, and the body can also make it. This is different from taking isolated glycine.

forms.name: Isolated glycine
forms.note: Sold as an amino-acid powder or in capsules. This is not a complete protein source.

forms.name: Combination products
forms.note: Products combining glycine with NAC or other ingredients have different compositions from glycine alone. Findings about a mixture cannot be assigned to glycine by itself.

reference.noUpperLimit: This basic guide does not provide reference intakes or upper-limit values.

cautions: Being a normal part of proteins does not establish that concentrated supplements are safe in every circumstance. This guide does not establish long-term supplement safety.
Blood-level associations with metabolic disease are not a diagnosis of glycine deficiency and are not instructions to treat a condition with glycine.
This guide has not assessed medicine interactions or safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding or children; an empty interaction list is not confirmation that every combination is safe.

sources.title: Glycine Metabolism and Its Alterations in Obesity and Metabolic Diseases.
